title: Clipping
kicker: ENCT 201 · Computer Graphics and Visualization · Chapter 2 (clipping)
subtitle: Do not draw what you cannot see: find the part of each line that lies inside the window.

sections.title: Why clip
sections.body: Anything outside the window is wasted effort (and could overflow the frame buffer). Clipping removes it before rasterising. The design goal: decide most cases — fully inside, fully outside — very cheaply, and compute intersections only when needed.

questions.prompt: Main purpose of clipping is to…

choices.text: Discard geometry outside the window before drawing it.

sections.title: Cohen–Sutherland
sections.body: Give each endpoint a 4-bit outcode (Top, Bottom, Right, Left): a bit is 1 if the point lies beyond that edge. If both codes are 0000 — trivially accept. If the AND of the codes is non-zero — both ends are beyond the same edge — trivially reject. Otherwise clip the outside endpoint to one window edge by intersection and repeat. For the window (10,10)–(50,50) the line (0,20)–(60,40) clips to 10,23.33 50,36.67.

worked.why: P1 = (0,20) is left of x = 10: outcode 0001. P2 = (60,40) is right of x = 50: outcode 0010.
AND = 0000, OR ≠ 0000: undecided, so clip. Intersection with x = 10: y = 20 + (40−20)·(10−0)/(60−0).

problems.prompt: Clip the line (0,20)–(60,40) against the window x,y ∈ [10,50].
problems.answer: Result 10,23.33 50,36.67 (left edge at y≈23.33, right edge at y≈36.67).

sections.title: Liang–Barsky
sections.body: Write the line as P(t) = P₁ + t·(P₂ − P₁), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Each window edge gives an inequality t·p ≤ q with p = −Δx, Δx, −Δy, Δy and q = x₁ − xmin, xmax − x₁, …. Where p < 0 the line enters: raise t₀ to max(q/p); where p > 0 it leaves: lower t₁ to min(q/p). If t₀ > t₁ the line is outside. Faster than Cohen–Sutherland because it computes at most one intersection per end. Same example: 10,23.33 50,36.67.

choices.text: No part of the line is inside the window.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The entering point comes after the leaving point.

figures.caption: Figure 2.8.1 — Liang–Barsky
figures.note: Watch t₀ rise and t₁ fall.

sections.title: Polygon and text clipping
sections.body: Clipping a polygon must produce a polygon, not loose lines. Sutherland–Hodgman clips against one window edge at a time, keeping inside vertices and adding intersection points; it is right for convex polygons and can leave extra edges for concave ones, which Weiler–Atherton handles by walking the boundaries. Text is clipped per character (all-or-none), per string, or per pixel (most exact).

questions.prompt: Which algorithm clips concave polygons correctly?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It follows the polygon and window boundaries, allowing several output pieces.

sections.title: Point clipping
sections.body: A point (x, y) is inside the window iff xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax and ymin ≤ y ≤ ymax. Everything else builds on this test.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Cohen–Sutherland: outcodes, accept/reject fast, else clip an edge at a time.
  • Liang–Barsky: parametric t₀…t₁ interval, fewer intersections.
